song.title: Glasshouse Groove
song.summary: An original percussive pop fingerstyle piece in drop‑D. The low D string drones as a kick‑drum bass while the thumb slaps a snare backbeat on 2 and 4, and a chiming natural‑harmonic hook (F#–D–A–B, played at the 7th and 12th frets) acts as the chorus. It moves from a sparse groove to a fuller second verse, a contrasting B section built on the IV chord with a borrowed bVI colour, and then a climax that brings back the hook over full slap‑and‑knock drums with a 32nd‑note fill. It ends on a strummed D chord and a ringing harmonic chord. Light reharmonization only: sus4 dominants, maj7 colours and one borrowed Bbmaj7.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bars 1–2 play the 'glass' hook as natural harmonics over the knock-and-slap cell, with the low D drone left ringing underneath. Bar 2 answers with a G4+B4 harmonic pair that hints at the Gmaj7 coming in bar 3. Bars 3–4 switch to fretted shapes and play each chord change an 8th early. The A7sus4 bar ends with a string-3 2h4 hammer over a C# (string 2, fret 2), then an 8th rest so that C#→D and B→A resolve into the A section's D.

sections.name: A
sections.note: The fretted melody (F#–E–D–E–F#–A) sits over the knock/slap groove, and every chord change is anticipated on the 'and' of 4 by the melody note: A4 into Bm7, G4 into Gmaj7 and Em7, E4 into A7sus4. Bar 5 brings the glass harmonic hook back to open the second phrase, and the A–G–F# pull-off triplet in bar 8 lands on F#, the melody's starting note for A′.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: Every phrase starts on the 'and' of 4 of the bar before. The muted thumb ghost on the 'e' of 3 makes the groove feel busier. Bar 5 plays the glass hook as fretted notes an octave lower (F#–D–A–B, answered by open G+B on beat 4). Bar 8 slides up string 3 into C#, the 3rd of A7, to push hard into B's Gmaj7.

sections.name: B
sections.note: B is where the piece takes a breath. The only drum hit is a slap on beat 4, so let every note ring: open B and E sit in unison with fretted B3 and E4 to make the campanella shimmer, and the G4+B4 harmonics at the end of bar 4 echo the hook's answer. Bar 7's low Bb (string 6, 8th fret) keeps the A4 melody note from bar 6 as a common tone. Bar 8 is the opposite: open A7sus4 chops with 16th slaps that grow into a full strum, ending on G (the 7th) to push into the D climax.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: The hook comes back in full in bars 1 and 5, and its held B4 is now a harp harmonic (fret string 3 at fret 4, touch fret 16, pluck). Under it the thumb plays 16ths that never stop, with knocks on beat 1 and the 'and' of 2. In hook bars the second knock moves one 16th later, to the 'a' of 2, so your right hand is free for the harmonic. The melody is the A melody up the octave. Let the hammer-ons and pull-offs fall on the slaps and knocks. The tapped fill in bar 4 and the 32nd-note run from G5 down to C#5 in bar 8 are the two big moments. Bar 8 ends with tenths stepping down by half steps (A/C#, then G#/C) into the G and B of the Outro's Gmaj7.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: The hook plays one last time over a low G, and its held B4 becomes a harp harmonic (fret string 3 at 4 and touch fret 16). Slaps now land only on beat 3, which slows the cadence. A quick D-shape rasgueado flick on the 'and' of 4 in bar 38 sets up the full drop‑D strum. The piece ends on a 12th‑fret harmonic chime over low D, and a final slap on beat 4 mutes the bass as the last hit.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap goes
tasteNotes.body: Slap on beats 2 and 4 with the side of the thumb landing across strings 5–6 near the end of the fretboard, then bounce off straight away. Never pluck strings 5 or 6 on those beats. The 16th low‑D pickup on the 'a' of 2 is what makes the groove sound 'pop': it pushes beat 3 like a kick drum. Do the body knock on beat 1 with the heel of the palm or the middle finger just below the bridge.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the harmonic hook
tasteNotes.body: Learn the four harmonics as a chord map first: 7th fret on strings 2, 3 and 4, then 12th fret on string 2. Touch the string exactly above the fret wire, pluck near the bridge, and lift the finger as soon as you pluck. Practise the hook with a metronome at 70 BPM with only the beat‑2 slap, then add the knock, then the drone. Let the B4 ring through the beat‑4 slap.

tasteNotes.title: Drop‑D keeps the bass moving smoothly
tasteNotes.body: With low D as a drone, every chord change in A and A′ only moves the upper voices: D to Bm7 to Gmaj7 to A7sus4 shares the A or D on top. The sus4 to 3 resolution (D to C#) is saved for A′ bar 8 and Climax bar 8, so the full A7 sounds like a release. In B, Bbmaj7 slides down a half step to A7sus4 on string 6 (8th fret to 7th fret).

tasteNotes.title: Dynamic arc
tasteNotes.body: Think of the dynamics as one fifth of the performance. Intro: sparse, about mf. A: steady. A′: busier with ghost notes. B: pull back to mp with open strings ringing and half‑time drums. Climax: everything at once. Outro: one big strum, then the harmonics ring out. When you film it, the dynamic changes between sections are what keep viewers watching.

tasteNotes.title: Reference listening
tasteNotes.body: For slap placement and hook‑driven pop arrangements, listen to Sungha Jung's pop covers. For drop‑D harmonics used as a melodic hook, listen to Mike Dawes's 'Somebody That I Used to Know'. For a groove made of a kick knock plus a 16th bass pickup, listen to Kent Nishimura's arrangements. For tapped fills and dynamic builds, listen to Marcin's 'Kashmir'.

song.title: Amazing Grace — Sunday Night Sway (Gospel Neo-Soul Chord-Melody)
song.summary: This plays Amazing Grace in D with the melody exactly as the hymn goes. It is tuned to drop D so a low open D can ring under every phrase like a church organ pedal. The piece is 40 bars and follows the hymn's 16-bar verse: the first half is A, the second half is A′, B brings back the first half an octave higher over minor chords, and the Climax brings back the second half with the fullest playing. The hymn's simple three chords are swapped for lush 9th and 13th chords (maj9, m9, 13sus4) and church-style moves like Gm6 to Dmaj9 (the "Amen" sound). The arc is: soft opening, a gentle swaying verse, a darker middle, a full gospel climax, and a ringing harmonic ending. A short 'Grace Lick' (a slide into the melody, a hammer-on and a harmonic) closes every section and ties the piece together.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bars 1–3 sit over the open low D (drop-D) while the top voice walks down F#–E–D. Each bar's small hammer-on adds the neo-soul 9th-to-3rd colour. Bar 4 ends the walk on C#: the dyad slides into the D of A13sus4, then pulls off to B and hammers to C# for A13. The fret-12 harmonics chime, and the pickup A (string 3, fret 2) on beat 3 leads into Dmaj9.

sections.name: A
sections.note: Keep it sparse and singing at mp. Each bar has just the thumb bass on 1 and a soft pinch on 2, with no hammer-ons yet, and the long notes slide in from a fret below: 'grace' (F#), 'sound' (A, with the bass on string 5) and 'me' (A). Bar 8 plays the Grace Lick over A: the F#+A dyad slides from 6/4 to 7/5, then string 3 hammers from 4 to 6 (B to C#, the 9th rising to the 3rd), the fret-12 chime sounds on the 'and' of 2, and the pickup 'I' (A, string 3 fret 2) lands on beat 3. Damp the chime with your right palm as the pickup sounds so the melody stays on top going into A′.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: The Sway Cell now plays in full: listen for the E→F# hammer-on on string 4 on the 'and' of 2, and for the chromatic line B→B♭→A on string 3 that takes 'now am found' through Gm6 into Dmaj9/A. The section ends with an 'Amen' (Gm6/D), the Grace Lick climbing up the neck to D–G–B harmonics at fret 12, and a pickup A on string 2, fret 10, which puts your hand in place for the B section's high melody.

sections.name: B
sections.note: Section B sets "Amazing grace… like me" an octave up on the top string, with D5 at fret 10, F#5 at 14 and A5 at 17. Under it, the bass walks down B–A–G–F#, so the hymn's tonic notes turn into the dark 3rd and 5th of Bm9, and the A in bar 4 becomes the gritty #9 of F#7#9. Bars 2 and 6 change chord on the 'and' of 3. Bar 6 also changes tone colour: F#5 is a harp harmonic and E5 a natural harmonic over open-string Em11. Bar 7 holds the high A with vibrato. Bar 8 plays the Grace Lick quietly over an open A bass instead of the low D drone. On beat 3 it drops to A7b9, with F#4 on top as the pickup on "I" leading into the Climax's Dmaj9.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: Each downbeat is a fast thumb-to-index roll of a 4–5-note grip, with a hammer on the 'and' of 2 (9th to 3rd: E–F# in bars 1, 4 and 5, A–B in bar 2, C–C# in A13) and a thumb ghost on the 'and' of 3. Listen for the half-step inner moves (D#→D into Em9, B♭→A in the A7b9 pull-off) and for bar 7's hammer-on run, which carries 'see' from D4 up to D5. To make room for the grips, 'am' is shortened to an eighth note so Gm6 can enter, and 'found/was' moves up an octave to A4.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: Outro, bars 37–40, played slower and slower: the last 'now I see' (F#–E–D) is played in harmonics: string 2 at fret 7, string 1 at fret 12, then string 4 at fret 5. Under them, the E→F# hammer-on and then a B♭→A pull-off over Gm6/D give the plagal 'Amen'. After a slow rolled Dmaj9 up to a high F# with vibrato, the Grace Lick gets one last stretched-out play: slide the F#+B dyad from frets 6 to 7, hammer E to F# on string 3 (frets 9 to 11), then strike the fret-12 chime on strings 1–3 with the open low D and let it all fade to silence.

tasteNotes.title: Gm6 → Dmaj9: the half-step 'Amen'
tasteNotes.body: The church sound in the A′ and Climax cadences comes from one inner voice: B-flat (the minor 3rd of Gm6) falls to A (the 5th of D). At the same time E holds over as the 9th, and G falls to F#. Keep your fingers as close as possible here and only move the notes that change. The low D drone means the bass never moves, so all the emotion sits in that half step.

tasteNotes.title: Slides that sing, not smear
tasteNotes.body: Slide into melody notes from exactly one fret below, starting slightly before the beat so the target lands on the beat. Only the A section's long notes ('grace', 'sound', 'me') get slides. If every note slides, none of them stand out. Keep pressure light during the slide and press down firmly on arrival.

tasteNotes.title: The 9-to-3 hammer is the neo-soul fingerprint
tasteNotes.body: The E-to-F# hammer-on on string 4 (frets 2 to 4) in the Sway Cell plays the 9th resolving to the 3rd. That is the vocal 'bend' gospel singers use. Hold it back for the whole A section so that when it arrives in A′ it sounds like the choir coming in.

tasteNotes.title: Practise the Grace Lick on its own first
tasteNotes.body: Loop the one-bar Grace Lick at 60 bpm: slide on beat 1, hammer-on on the 'and' of 2, harmonics on beat 3. Play the fret-12 harmonics by lightly touching strings 1–3 directly above the fret wire with one finger flat across them, then lift as you pluck. The low D must keep ringing underneath, so let the thumb rest away from string 6.

tasteNotes.title: Feel 3/4 like a slow 6/8
tasteNotes.body: Count '1-and-2-and-3-and' but lean on beat 1 and let beats 2 and 3 float slightly late. That lazy pull is the sway. Practise with a metronome clicking only on beat 1 at 72 bpm so you learn to place the swing yourself.

tasteNotes.title: Listening
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Cory Henry's organ reharmonizations of hymns for the chord colours. Listen to Isaiah Sharkey and Melanie Faye for neo-soul hammer-on licks on guitar. Listen to Tommy Emmanuel's solo hymn medleys for how to keep a drone bass and melody independent in a chord-melody arrangement.

song.title: House of the Rising Sun — Dark Arpeggio Blues Fingerstyle
song.summary: A one-guitar showpiece built on the famous 6/8 A-minor arpeggio. The traditional melody (in its familiar Animals-era form) stays on top and isn't changed. The piece starts quiet and moody, with plain open-string arpeggios, a chromatic bass walk (A–G–F#–F) and a harmonic chime. It then moves to a darker interlude on the iv chord (Dm), and finally a percussive last verse with a body knock on beat 1, a thumb slap on beat 4, passing bass notes and a fill at the end of each phrase. It ends on a rasgueado-style Am strum with a final harmonic chime. Everything is in standard tuning with no capo, so the open A, E and high-e strings can drone and keep the sound dark.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: The Chime Rise opens the piece softly. Its slide to the high A and the 12th-fret harmonics should ring into the thumb's chromatic walk down, A–G–F#–E, which falls one step per bar. Bars 2–4 use the bass, 3-2-1-2-3 rocking arpeggio that runs under the whole tune. Let the G# in bar 4 hang with vibrato so it pulls hard toward the Am of the first verse.

sections.name: A — Verse 1
sections.note: This is the quietest statement of the tune. The thumb keeps the plain root-and-5th cell going while the a finger plays each syllable on strings 1–2. From bar 13 the hammer-ons and the F-E and G-E-D# pull-offs build toward the end of the verse, and the harmonic chime on the last eighth of bar 20 carries straight into the Dm interlude.

sections.name: B — Interlude (Dark Contrast)
sections.note: The open A string keeps droning while the left hand moves between the fret-5 Dm barre and the fret-5 Am shape. A long slide up to the D at fret 10 leads into each falling D–C–A phrase, and the line climbs to the F barre at fret 8. Bar 26 ends on the harp harmonic on the low E and a string-1 triplet (open–4–5) that hammers onto A. Bar 27 brings back the Chime Rise with a G–F–E pull-off in the bass. In bar 28 the bass climbs E–F#–G# in 16ths, which pulls straight into the slapped Am at the start of the climax.

sections.name: Climax — Verse 2 (Percussive)
sections.note: Knock and bass on eighth 1, slap on eighth 4 in every bar. The chromatic walk A–G–F#–F (and later G–F#–F–E) moves up string 5 at frets 12–8, and the high-octave melody rides on string 1 above it. Bar 29 restates the Chime Rise. The four fills then grow, from a pull-off run (bar 32) to tapped harmonics (bar 36) to an open-string E–G#–B–E run (bar 40) and a rasgueado (bar 44). Melody note: this is a reconstruction of the vocal's rising and falling contour, written from memory and placed an octave up. Import a melody file if you want the exact sung notes.

sections.name: Outro — Big Ending
sections.note: The energy drops first: bar 45 plays Am at half speed, and bar 46 climbs an Fmaj7 up to the open high E. The ending then builds again: a slap, a body knock and a 16th-note open-string E7 run lead to G# (the leading tone), which resolves up to the high A in the final rasgueado. The fret-12 harmonic chime follows at once, and the low A carries a slow vibrato under both.

tasteNotes.title: The chromatic bass walk is the hidden second hook
tasteNotes.body: Am → C/G → D/F# → F produces a bass line that falls A–G–F#–F while the open B and E strings stay constant above it. It appears in the intro and returns in the climax, so the ear knows the peak is related to the opening. Use your thumb for C/G on string 6 at fret 3 and D/F# on string 6 at fret 2, and keep the upper strings ringing as the bass moves.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap and knock go in 6/8
tasteNotes.body: In 6/8 the backbeat is eighth 4 (the second dotted-quarter beat), not beats 2 and 4. Knock on the body under the soundhole with the side of the thumb on eighth 1 and play the bass on the same eighth. Slap strings 5–6 with the thumb on eighth 4 and don't pluck a bass note there. Practise the climax cell on open Am at 50 bpm until the slap sounds as loud as the melody note.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the Chime Rise harmonics
tasteNotes.body: Lay your ring finger flat across strings 3-2-1 directly over the 12th fret wire, touching the strings without pressing them down, and pluck p-i-m-a together. Lift the finger straight away. If the G string sounds dull, you are slightly on the fret side of the wire, so move toward the bridge. Practise slide (fret 5) → lift → chime until the move takes less than one eighth note.

tasteNotes.title: Keep it dark: avoid bright major sounds
tasteNotes.body: Play the E chord as a plain triad or E7 with the open low E. Don't add a 9th or 13th, because the hard G# leading tone gives the piece its blues-noir sound. In the interlude, let the Dm sit on the open A drone so the minor-6th note (F) clashes against the drone. That clash makes the sound darker than the verse.

tasteNotes.title: Reference recordings
tasteNotes.body: Listen to The Animals (1964) for the 6/8 arpeggio pulse and the organ-solo shape that the interlude follows. Listen to Dave Van Ronk's and Bob Dylan's early recordings for the rawer folk-blues version with the chromatic bass. For the percussive climax, study Mike Dawes and Kent Nishimura, who place slaps in compound time without the melody losing its legato.

song.title: Scarborough Fair — DADGAD Harp & Drone Setting
song.summary: This is a solo setting of Scarborough Fair in DADGAD, in D Dorian. The melody follows the familiar traditional/Simon & Garfunkel contour (Are you going to Scarborough Fair = D D A A E F E D), but it is not a note-for-note copy of any recording. The open D, A and D strings drone under every bar. The 3/4 lilt stays harp-like, and the piece builds like a story. The Intro sets out the hook: the first four melody notes played as ringing cross-string notes and capped by harp harmonics. Verse A is sparse, with only a bass note and the melody. B drops the melody into the thumb register under a high open-string drone so the second half of the tune sounds new. The Climax brings back the full verse with campanella runs, harp-harmonic answers at each phrase end and a fuller bass. The Outro repeats the hook as a harmonic chime and ends on a slow rolled strum of the whole open tuning.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: The Scarborough chime (D–A–E–F) is played across different strings over a low-D bass, so each note keeps ringing into the next. Two harp harmonics (A, D) answer it. In bars 3–4 the C/D keeps the open D and A strings sounding, so it sounds like a Dorian drone rather than a real chord change. Hold the final D in bar 4 as a breath before the verse.

sections.name: A — Verse 1
sections.note: This verse is just the tune over a single bass note in each bar, so let the DADGAD open strings ring under it. The G-major bar (bar 11) brings in the Dorian B♮ with a hammer-on on 'rose-ma-ry'. The verse ends with the Scarborough chime and two harp harmonics answering 'true love of mine'.

sections.name: B — Low Verse (contrast)
sections.note: The thumb plays the second half of the tune ('Remember me… true love of mine') on the 4th string, sliding down the neck from fret 12 to the open string like a cello line. Meanwhile i and m keep an unbroken eighth-note drone on the open A and D strings. Start at p and swell from bar 25, where the thumb sweeps across the open D–A–D bass strings. Bar 28 lands on 'mine' and climbs out through the G–A–B♮ hammer triplet to the open high D, ready for the Climax.

sections.name: Climax — Verse 2
sections.note: The melody moves up to strings 1–2 (D4–D5) over the full harp-lilt cell: bass on 1, open-4th drone on the & of 1, open-A fills, with a bass pickup on beat 3 into each new phrase. Listen for the harp-harmonic echoes after each phrase-end note and the campanella runs in bars 36, 40 and 44. Bar 44 gives you a full Dm strum and then the hook as harmonics (D–A–E–F). Its campanella run lands on A3, which leads into the Outro chime.

sections.name: Outro — Chime & Strum
sections.note: Slow down a little more in each bar. The 12th-fret chime in bar 45 and the 7th-fret C/D chime in bar 46 hint at the ♭VII over the low D drone that never stops. The Dm roll in bar 47 is played as single 16ths from low to high and left to ring, and the piece ends on a 12th-fret harmonic chord with F on the 5th string at fret 8 for the minor colour. Hold that last chord until it fades out.

tasteNotes.title: Dorian lives in the G-major chord
tasteNotes.body: In D Dorian the B♮ is the one note that separates the tune from plain D minor. Give it room in bar 7 of each verse ('…mary and thyme'). Fret the low G on the 6th string at fret 5 and let the melody's B ring against the open D drones. If that bar sounds bright and slightly unexpected, you're doing it right. Don't change it to B♭.

tasteNotes.title: Harp harmonics, practised in slow motion
tasteNotes.body: Lightly touch the string 12 frets above the fretted (or open) note with the right-hand index finger, then pluck behind it with the ring finger (a). Thumb and fretting hand keep the drone going. First practise the two-note answer in the hook alone: 1st string open (touch at fret 12) and 2nd string fret 7 (touch at fret 19). Use a metronome at 60 and play them as two quarter notes. Then alternate them with regular plucked notes so you get the harp effect where harmonics and normal notes ring together.

tasteNotes.title: Campanella = no two neighbouring notes on the same string
tasteNotes.body: For the 16th-note runs in the Climax, finger each scale step on a different string. For example, D (1st string, open), C (2nd string, fret 3), B♮ (3rd string, fret 4), A (2nd string, open), G (3rd string, open), F (4th string, fret 3), E (4th string, fret 2). Every note overlaps the next and the run sounds like a harp glissando. Plan these fingerings before you add speed.

tasteNotes.title: Shape the dynamic arc on purpose
tasteNotes.body: Record the whole piece and check that it matches this curve: Intro mp, A mp with only the bass and melody, B p (the deepest dip), Climax growing to f at bar 44, then the Outro chiming quietly before the final strum, which should be the loudest single gesture. On camera the B section's restraint is what makes the Climax hit.

tasteNotes.title: Reference players
tasteNotes.body: Pierre Bensusan for DADGAD drones and modal phrasing. Tony McManus ('Ceol More') for Celtic ornaments and harp-like campanella. Martin Simpson's traditional English settings for how to let a ballad melody breathe over open strings. Also Simon & Garfunkel's 'Scarborough Fair/Canticle' for the vocal phrasing and lilt. The melody here follows the familiar contour but makes no claim to note-for-note accuracy.

song.title: Jingle Bells — Drop-D Slap & Chime
song.summary: The chorus is moved up a whole step to D and played in drop-D. That puts the melody on the top two strings in first position and lets the open low D act like a kick drum under it. Bars 1–4 set up a pop groove: a body knock on beat 1, a thumb slap on beats 2 and 4, and eighth notes on the inner strings. The harmony is reworked as I–vi–ii9–Vsus4–V–I. Bars 5–8 get busier, with sixteenth notes and a walking D/F# bass. The usual D7 becomes a V9/V chord, which comes out as E9 in this key. The piece ends with a slide up to a 7th-position D chord and a harmonic chime at the 7th fret. Every melody note is kept exactly as written, just transposed up a whole step.

sections.name: A — Groove (bars 1–4)
sections.note: The thumb alternates between the low bass on 1 and 3 and slaps on 2 and 4, while the melody stays on the open-position top strings. Bar 4 is the hook: a 7th-fret harmonic D chord, then a pull-off run down the high E string that leads into bar 5.

sections.name: B — Climax & Chime (bars 5–8)
sections.note: This section is busier: sixteenth-note inner voices, a walking D/F# bass, and an E9 that leans into the turnaround. The ending slides into a 7th-position D chord, then you lighten the same fingers so the strings ring as harmonics.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap and knock go
tasteNotes.body: Knock the lower bout with your thumb-side palm on beat 1 while your thumb plays the bass. On beats 2 and 4, slap the wound strings with the side of your thumb. Keep the slap as one quick motion with no follow-through, so the treble melody note on that beat (bars 1–2, beat 2) still rings. Never pluck strings 5 or 6 on a slap beat. The bass parts are written to leave those beats free.

tasteNotes.title: The 7th-fret D-chord chime
tasteNotes.body: In drop-D, the 7th-fret natural harmonics on strings 4, 3 and 2 make an A–D–F# triad. That's a full D major chord with no fretting. Lay one finger very lightly across all three strings directly above the fret wire, pick them together, then lift the finger right away. In bar 8 your fingers are already at fret 7 after the slide. Just ease off the pressure and pluck again, and the fretted D turns into the chime.

tasteNotes.title: Bar 4 pull-off cascade
tasteNotes.body: Before beat 4, put your pinky on fret 5, ring finger on fret 3 and middle finger on fret 2, all on the high E string. Slap and pick the fret-5 note at the same moment. Then pull off three times, 5→3→2→0, flicking each finger slightly toward the floor. That gives A–G–F#–E. The open E leads straight into the G melody note on the downbeat of bar 5. Practise it slowly against a metronome so it lands as even sixteenths.

tasteNotes.title: Pop reharmonisation that keeps the melody intact
tasteNotes.body: The original chorus stays mostly on the I chord. Here it becomes I–vi7–ii9–Vsus4–V. D to Bm7 only moves the bass, since the top of the D shape stays put. In the Em9 bar the F# melody becomes the 9th, the bar's D melody note becomes the sus4 of A, and the suspension resolves to C# just as the melody steps to E. The usual D7 in bar 7 is played as E9 here, so the melody's F# is its 9th. That makes the V/V chord sound modern instead of barbershop.

tasteNotes.title: Reference sound
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Sungha Jung's and Kent Nishimura's holiday covers for the kick-and-snare thumb feel. Listen to Tommy Emmanuel's live Christmas medleys for how a melody stays out in front of a busy thumb. Pay attention to how quietly the accompaniment notes are played compared with the melody. That balance matters more than speed.

song.title: Ode to Joy (Percussive Pop Fingerstyle)
song.summary: Beethoven's theme is moved up a major third to E major and played with a capo at 4, so you finger easy open C-shapes and the open strings ring out. The harmony is reworked as a pop progression: I–IV | V–iii7 | vi–IVmaj7 | I–V, then the same again ending V7–I. That gives the hymn a modern singer-songwriter feel. Your thumb plays the bass on 1 and 3 and slaps the low strings on 2 and 4. Body knocks on the 16th note before beat 3 work as a kick drum, and hammer-ons in the inner voices fill the gaps. Bar 4 ends with a 12th-fret harmonic chime as the hook. The second half gets busier with 16th-note fills, a slide, and a hammer-on landing on a slap. It ends with a run of harp harmonics over the final chord.

sections.name: A: Groove
sections.note: The melody stays on strings 1–2 in open position, and the thumb alternates between bass notes on 1 and 3 and slaps on 2 and 4. Keep this half fairly light so the second half has somewhere to grow. The 12th-fret harmonic chord at the end of bar 4 is the hook.

sections.name: A': Climax & Harp-Harmonic Ending
sections.note: This half uses the same thumb pattern, but the inner voices move in 16ths, the melody slides into G (bar 5), and the D in bar 6 is hammered on at the same moment as the slap. The C chord arrives an 8th early in bar 8. After that, harp harmonics finish the piece.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap goes
tasteNotes.body: On beats 2 and 4, bring the side of your thumb down onto strings 5–6 near the end of the fingerboard so it snaps against the frets like a snare. At the same moment, pluck the melody with i/m. Never pluck strings 5–6 on those beats, because the slap mutes them anyway. On beats 1 and 3, the thumb plays the actual bass note (C, G, E, A, F shapes). Those alternating jobs are the whole groove.

tasteNotes.title: The 12th-fret chime hook (bar 4)
tasteNotes.body: In bar 4, let the D on beat 3 ring with a little vibrato. Then lay your index finger lightly across strings 4–2 directly over the 12th fret (relative to the capo, so fret 16 on the neck). Pluck those strings on the beat-4 slap. You get a G-chord bell that echoes the melody's D. Practise just the move from fret 3 to the harmonics until it lands in time with no gap.

tasteNotes.title: Harp-harmonic ending
tasteNotes.body: In bar 8, hold the C shape. Touch each string 12 frets above its fretted note with your right index finger (string 4 at 14, string 3 at 12, string 2 at 13, string 1 at 12, all relative to the capo). Pluck with your ring finger, one string per 16th note. On the final eighth, your thumb plucks the low C on string 5 at the same moment as the last harmonic on string 2, so the tonic bass sits under the chime.

tasteNotes.title: Pop reharm with inner-voice motion
tasteNotes.body: Instead of the textbook I–V, the melody sits over I–IV | V–iii7 | vi–IVmaj7. In bar 3, the D over the A shape is a 6th, and then the open-E melody note turns it into a full maj7. In bars 2 and 6, the bass walks E–B–A from the iii7 into the vi. The hammer-ons on string 4 (D→E) keep the 16ths moving without crowding the tune.

tasteNotes.title: Build it in layers
tasteNotes.body: Start at 70 bpm with thumb only: bass, slap, bass, slap. Add the melody on top. Then add the body knock on the 16th before beat 3, using the heel of your picking hand on the lower bout. Add the hammer-ons last. In bar 6, the D is hammered on while you slap, so the left hand supplies the note and the right hand supplies the snare. Slow that bar down on its own until the two line up exactly.

tasteNotes.title: Listening
tasteNotes.body: Sungha Jung's pop covers show the same slap-on-2-and-4 groove under a simple melody. Kent Nishimura's arrangements are good for clean harp-harmonic endings, and Mike Dawes's 'Somebody That I Used to Know' cover shows the harmonic tricks pushed further.

song.title: Twinkle Twinkle Little Star – Percussive Pop Fingerstyle
song.summary: The nursery rhyme is moved up a major third to E major. This lets the open low E and A strings drive a modern percussive groove: a body knock on beat 1, thumb slaps on 2 and 4, and a busy thumb line under the melody, which always stays on top on the first two strings. Section A keeps the familiar I–IV–V harmony and introduces the signature move, a 12th-fret harmonic chime in the gap after the long note. It ends with an open-string hammer-on run that slides into the second phrase. Section B adds pop colour chords (E/G#, C#m7 with a common-tone move to Amaj7, G#m7), 7th-fret harmonics, a chromatic walk-up in the bass and a triplet roll. It ends on a big Eadd9 strum and a three-string harmonic chime. The melody is exact; the chords are a tasteful reharmonization.

sections.name: A – Groove & Chime
sections.note: Get the knock–slap backbeat steady under a plain melody first. The 12th-fret chime in bar 2 is the hook, and bar 4's open-string hammer-on run (0-2-4 on the high E string) slides straight into bar 5.

sections.name: B – Climax & Chime Ending
sections.note: Fuller texture: more 16th-note motion underneath, colour chords (C#m7 to Amaj7 keeps G# and E on the inner strings), 7th-fret harmonics and a chromatic B–C–C# bass walk-up in bar 6. It ends with a full Eadd9 strum and a harmonic chime on strings 6, 2 and 1.

tasteNotes.title: Knock on 1, slap on 2 and 4
tasteNotes.body: On every beat 1, tap the side of the guitar top near the bridge with the heel of your picking hand while your thumb plucks the bass note. That knock is the kick drum. On beats 2 and 4, bounce the side of your thumb onto strings 6–5 near the end of the fingerboard so they click against the frets. Bass notes are never written on a slap beat, so your thumb is always free for it. Practise bars 1 and 3 with just the knock, the slap and the bass until the backbeat feels automatic, then add the melody.

tasteNotes.title: The harmonic hook (bars 2, 6 and 8)
tasteNotes.body: Each long melody note leaves a gap on beat 4, and that is where the chime goes. In bar 2, lightly touch strings 1–2 right over the 12th fret with your fretting hand while the picking thumb slaps. Then lift your hand straight away so the chime rings. Bar 6 uses the same move at the 7th fret (F#5 and B5 over the B chord). The ending adds string 6 at the 12th fret. Pluck strings 6, 2 and 1 together for an open-fifth E chime.

tasteNotes.title: Bar 4 run into bar 5
tasteNotes.body: Pluck the open G string, hammer on to fret 1, then slap with the open B string. On the high E string, play it open, hammer on to fret 2 with your index finger and to fret 4 with your ring finger. Without picking again, slide the ring finger up to fret 7 for the B4 that starts bar 5. That slide is the first note of the phrase, so let it land right on the knock. Practise the hammer-ons in a loop at 70 bpm before bringing it up to tempo.

tasteNotes.title: Common tones in the reharmonization
tasteNotes.body: C#m7 (x46457) to Amaj7 (x06655) keeps G# on string 4 and E on string 2. Only the bass, the G string and the melody move, so the colour change sounds smooth rather than jumpy. The chromatic B–C–C# bass at the end of bar 6 walks into C#m7. Bring that bass out a little; it is the moment the climax starts.

tasteNotes.title: Melody first, then the groove
tasteNotes.body: Play the melody alone (the top note of each knock or slap beat) until it sings, then add the thumb. The melody is always the highest note when it starts, so if it gets buried, play the inner 8th and 16th notes more softly instead of digging in harder on top.

tasteNotes.title: Reference players
tasteNotes.body: For the knock-and-slap pocket under a simple melody, listen to Sungha Jung's arrangements of children's songs and pop covers. Hear how Kent Nishimura's percussive covers fit harmonics into the gaps in a phrase. Tommy Emmanuel's 'Angelina' shows harmonic chimes used as an ending.
